claim.pdf_says: 3.111 internal data / all data described in a source unit except external data and external file connectors; 3.112 key of reference / key, either prime or alternate, currently being used to access records within an indexed file; 3.113 line delimiter; ... ten consecutive definition entries 3.111-3.120 set as ordinary body text on one page, with NO horizontal rule anywhere on the page.
claim.markdown_says: / ## Page 44 / # ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E) / --- / **3.111** **internal data** ... a `---` thematic break inserted after the running header and after EVERY ONE of the ten entries 3.111-3.120; eleven spurious rules in total on this page, at ISO_COBOL.md lines 1994, 2000, 2006, 2014, 2020, 2026, 2032, 2038, 2045, 2051, 2057.
claim.why_it_matters: `---` is the transcription's reserved page-break separator: elsewhere in ISO_COBOL.md it appears exactly once per page, immediately before the `` anchor. Page 44 emits eleven additional `---` rules INSIDE the page. No normative text is lost, but any consumer that segments the markdown on `---` (the reconciliation slicer, a chunker, a diff-by-page tool) will see eleven phantom page boundaries in the middle of clause 3 and mis-attribute entries 3.111-3.120 to eleven different 'pages'. The rules also render as horizontal lines that are not in the PDF.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED. The two verifiable facts the claim asserts are literally true but inert; the premise that makes them a defect is false, and the named harm does not exist. (1) Facts that do check out. The rendered PDF page (E:/Temp/specrecon/v44/spec_p44.png, 300 dpi) shows entries 3.111-3.120 as ordinary body text separated by vertical whitespace only, with no horizontal rule anywhere on the page. And ISO_COBOL.md does carry eleven `---` lines inside page 44, at exactly the eleven line numbers cited (1994, 2000, 2006, 2014, 2020, 2026, 2032, 2038, 2045, 2051, 2057). So far the claim quotes both sources correctly. (2) The premise is false. The claim's whole case rests on '`---` is the transcription's reserved page-break separator: elsewhere in ISO_COBOL.md it appears exactly once per page, immediately before the anchor.' A file-wide count refutes this three ways. ISO_COBOL.md contains 808 `---` lines against 1261 page anchors, so `---` cannot be a once-per-page marker -- most pages have no preceding rule at all. Only 514 of the 808 rules sit within three lines of an anchor; the remaining 294 are mid-page. Those 294 in-page rules are spread over 236 distinct pages. In-page `---` is therefore an ordinary, pervasive feature of this transcription, not a page-44 anomaly. (3) Page 44 is not even unusual within its own clause. Pages 35, 36 and 49 -- all clause 3 definition pages -- use the identical style: a `---` after the running header and one after each definition entry (10, 10 and 11 rules respectively; page 49 ties page 44 for the file-wide maximum). Page 44 is a member of that set, not an outlier. What actually exists is a cosmetic inconsistency INSIDE clause 3: pages 35/36/44/49 separate definition entries with rules while pages 37-43 and 45-48 use blank lines. That is a style inconsistency in the transcription, not a discrepancy against the PDF's content. (4) The stated harm is disproved by reading the named consumer. The claim asserts 'the reconciliation slicer' will see eleven phantom page boundaries. It will not. scripts/spec/page_workunit.py:33-44 segments purely on anchors: `open_re = re.compile(rf'^\s*$')` and `next_re = re.compile(r'^\s*$')`; its docstring states 'Markdown between and the next page anchor.' `---` is never matched. The slice this very verification consumed was correctly bounded and contained all eleven rules inside one page-44 unit, which is direct empirical proof. A hypothetical third-party chunker that split on `---` would already be broken by the other 283 in-page rules on 235 other pages; page 44 adds nothing new. (5) No content is at stake, as the claim itself concedes. Content parity is complete: all ten headwords and definition bodies are present and correct (3.111 internal data, 3.112 key of reference, 3.113 line delimiter with its 'Note 1 to entry: The line delimiter is implementor-defined.', 3.114 little-endian, 3.115 locale, 3.116 lock mode, 3.117 low-order end, 3.118 message control system with its admitted term MCS, 3.119 message-server, 3.120 message-tag). Nothing normative is added, lost or altered. This lands squarely on two of the stated rejection criteria: the difference is only formatting furniture, and the claim misquotes the markdown by asserting a file-wide `---` convention that the file does not follow. Nothing here can change how any spec question is adjudicated.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy. The eleven `---` lines on page 44 are real and the PDF page has no printed rules, but `---` is not a reserved page-break marker in ISO_COBOL.md: the file has 808 `---` against 1261 page anchors, and 294 of them are mid-page across 236 pages. Sibling clause-3 definition pages 35, 36 and 49 use the same entry-separator style (10, 10, 11 rules). The alleged harm is disproved by the code: scripts/spec/page_workunit.py:33-44 slices on `` anchors and never matches `---`. All ten entries 3.111-3.120 transcribe faithfully, including 3.113's Note 1 and 3.118's admitted term MCS. The only residue is a purely cosmetic style inconsistency within clause 3 (pages 35/36/44/49 rule-separate their entries; pages 37-43 and 45-48 do not), which is optional tidy-up, not a transcription defect.
